title: 3D Printing
desc: Learn to design, slice, print, finish and cost 3D-printed parts safely and sell them honestly.
outcomes: Prepare a model and slice it.
Print and finish a useful part.
task: Design or select a part, print it, finish it, test it against a requirement and cost it for sale.
condition: Access to a printer (own, makerspace or partner), a computer, free software, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Part meets the dimensions within 0.3 mm; print log shows settings; failure analysis written; safety rules followed; cost per part shown; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Makers, students, product designers, small manufacturers.
evidence: model, slicer settings, print log, test record, cost sheet
modules: Printers, materials and what suits what
Understand
The printer and material decide strength, detail, cost and safety. Choose from the need of the part.
Filament printers melt plastic and lay it in layers; resin printers cure liquid with light and give fine detail.
PLA is easy and stiff but softens in heat; PETG is tougher and handles moisture; ABS resists heat but gives off fumes and needs ventilation; flexible filaments make gaskets and grips.
Resins need gloves, washing and curing; waste resin is hazardous.
Check the maker's data sheet. Do not assume a printed part is food safe or load safe.
A shelf bracket is printed in PETG for toughness. A jewellery prototype is printed in resin for detail. A phone stand is printed in PLA because strength is not critical.
Compare four materials in a table for strength, heat, ease, cost and safety.
Table is accurate and cites data sheets.
Designing parts for printing
Apply
A model designed for printing prints well; a model copied from a metal part may not.
Wall thickness of at least two nozzle widths; avoid thin spikes.
Avoid overhangs steeper than about 45 degrees or add supports.
Layers pull apart most easily, so orient the part so loads run along the layer lines, not across them.
Add 0.2 to 0.4 mm clearance for moving or fitted parts.
A bracket printed on its side is much stronger than one printed upright because layer lines run along the load.
Design or choose a part, list dimensions, orientation and clearances.
Dimensions and orientation are justified in writing.
Slicing and settings
Apply
The slicer turns the model into printer instructions.
Layer height (0.1 to 0.3 mm), infill (10 to 40 per cent), walls, speed, temperature and supports.
Preview the tool path layer by layer before printing.
Save profiles for each material.
Check the first layer closely; most failures start there.
A part is sliced at 0.2 mm layers, 20 per cent infill and 3 walls. Print time is 2.5 hours and mass 38 g.
Slice your part and record all settings.
Settings are recorded and the preview shows no gaps.
Printing safely
Apply
Printers are hot, moving and sometimes unattended.
Place on a stable surface with good ventilation; keep flammable items away.
Do not touch the nozzle or bed when hot; tie back hair and loose clothes.
Do not leave long prints unattended without safeguards such as a smoke alarm.
Resin: wear gloves and eye protection and dispose of waste properly.
A smoke alarm and a fire blanket are kept near the printer; the print room has a window for airflow.
Print your part and keep a log of start, end, issues and temperatures.
Log is complete and safety kit is in place.
Troubleshooting failures
Analyse
Failures teach. Change one setting at a time and write down what happens.
Warping: use a heated bed, brim or enclosure.
Stringing: lower temperature or tune retraction.
Poor adhesion: clean the bed and level it.
Clogs: clean the nozzle and check filament moisture.
A large flat part warps at the corners. A heated bed at 60 degrees Celsius and a brim fix it on the next print.
Fix two issues and record the cause, change and result.
Notes show one change at a time.
Post-processing and finishing
Apply
Finishing makes a part usable and professional.
Remove supports, sand in steps, prime and paint where needed.
Resin parts: wash and cure fully before handling.
Check fit and trim.
Use a mask when sanding and spraying.
Sanding progressively from 120 to 400 grit gives a smooth surface suitable for painting.
Finish your part and photograph before and after.
Surface is smooth and fits.
Testing the part
Evaluate
A part is good only if it meets a requirement.
Measure with calipers and compare to the design.
Load test within safe limits; start low.
Test three copies to see variation.
Document the results.
Three bracket copies hold 4.8, 5.1 and 5.0 kg for 10 minutes without deflection.
Test three copies and report average and spread.
Results are recorded with units.
Costing and selling honestly
Create
Price covers material, time and risk of failures.
Material cost, power, machine wear, labour and failed prints.
Add 10 to 20 per cent for waste.
Disclose limits and intended use; do not sell safety-critical parts without testing.
Respect designs and licences; do not copy protected products.
Cost 62 INR for material and power (an estimate; check your market) plus 40 INR labour is 102 INR; adding 10 per cent for waste gives about 112 INR. The part sells for 150 INR.
Cost one part and write a short product note with limits.
Cost sheet is correct and the note states intended use.
rubric: Dimensions and load test results logged
Test repeated on a second print and spread recorded
Safety limits, food-contact rule and design rights are written down
Rules checked and a risky use refused in writing
